title: Walking the Camino
hook: hundreds of thousands walk to Santiago every year

segments.voice: Yesterday, blessing the house: chalk, water, and the words Jesus sent to the door. Your line was peace to this house. Did you stop on your threshold? Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

Buen camino. Two words, called out across a dusty road in northern Spain. A walker with a backpack passes a farmer leaning on a gate, and the farmer says it. Two strangers share a bench by a fountain, and as one heaves the pack back on, the other says it. A woman behind a café counter hands over a coffee and presses an ink stamp into a little booklet, and she says it too. In Spanish it means something like good way, or good road. And the road these walkers are on leads to a cathedral in a city called Santiago de Compostela. Today: walking the Camino.

The Camino de Santiago means the Way of Saint James. Tradition says the apostle James is buried in Santiago, and walkers come to his cathedral on foot along several routes. Some start at their own front doors. Some walk for prayer, some for grief, some to think, some without being sure why. Next, that word, way. In John's Gospel Jesus says, in the King James Bible, "I am the way, the truth, and the life." And in the book of Acts, before the name Christian shows up, Saul goes looking for followers of Jesus, "that if he found any of this way, whether they were men or women, he might bring them bound unto Jerusalem." This way. The early followers were people of the Way. So for some walkers, wishing a stranger a good way carries an echo of that. Then the road to Emmaus. On the day of the resurrection, two disciples walk out of Jerusalem, heartbroken, talking it over. "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them." They don't know him. He walks, listens, and opens the scriptures to them. At the village, evening coming on, they beg him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." At supper he breaks the bread, they know him, and he's gone. Then they say: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way?" Recognized afterward, looking back down the road. Last, the greeting itself. Some Camino walkers describe it this way: you don't choose your companions. The stranger who walks beside you for a morning, who shares water or a bandage, may be the one you remember. Catholics, Protestants, Orthodox Christians and people unsure what they believe can walk the same road, and buen camino doesn't ask which. It simply wishes you a good way.

Here's the practice: walk a long way on purpose, starting small. If you can, stand and walk slowly around the room, one step for each breath. Feel the heel, then the ball of the foot, then the toes. If you can't stand, press each foot into the floor in turn. Let each lap be a mile of road you haven't walked yet. If you pray, you can pray with your steps, a word or two from a psalm, or the name of someone you're carrying. If you don't, just count the steps and notice the feet that carry you. The bell holds the time.
Walking the Camino. The pilgrim road to Santiago, the Way of Saint James, where walkers wish each other buen camino.
Your line: buen camino. Today, take the longer way somewhere on foot, and wish one person a good way, in any words. Day one thousand three hundred seventy-four.

howItsDone: Pilgrims walk the Camino de Santiago on several routes across Spain and beyond, carrying a pilgrim's booklet stamped along the way, and some attend the pilgrims' Mass at the cathedral in Santiago when they arrive.

fork.setup: you're walking to Emmaus, heartbroken. a stranger has walked with you all afternoon and opened the scriptures. at the village he makes as if to go on. what do you do?
options: say goodbye at the edge of the village.
beg him to stay and eat with you.
walk faster to be rid of him.
fork.reveal: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening." at supper he breaks the bread, and they know him.

original.note: Greek: way, road. the word in John 14:6, "I am the way," and in Acts for the people of the Way.

trapdoor: what you thought: a long hike across Spain.
what it means: a pilgrim road to Santiago, where tradition places the tomb of James, walked as prayer, with strangers.
what a scholar hears: hodos, the way: the early followers were people of "this way," and at Emmaus Jesus was known afterward, "by the way."
recall: Catholic and Orthodox word for it
